questionText: What are REST principles? How would you design a RESTful API for a blog platform?
idealAnswer: REST principles: statelessness, client-server separation, uniform interface, cacheable responses. For a blog: GET /posts, POST /posts, GET /posts/:id, PUT/PATCH/DELETE /posts/:id. Use nouns not verbs, proper HTTP status codes (200, 201, 400, 404, 500). Versioning: /v1/posts. Pagination: cursor-based or ?page=1&limit=20.

questionText: Explain JWT-based authentication. What are its advantages and security pitfalls?
idealAnswer: JWT: header.payload.signature (Base64 encoded). Server signs with secret key; client sends in Authorization header. Stateless — no DB lookup per request. Pitfalls: can't invalidate before expiry (use short TTL + refresh tokens), store in httpOnly cookie not localStorage (XSS), prefer RS256 over HS256 for microservices.

questionText: Explain database indexing. How do B-tree indexes work? When should you NOT add an index?
idealAnswer: B-tree index: balanced tree where leaves are sorted by key. Lookup O(log n). Write overhead: every INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE must update the index tree. Do NOT index when: high write-to-read ratio, low cardinality columns (booleans), rarely queried columns, small tables. Composite indexes: column order matters — (a,b) index helps (a) queries but not (b) alone. Covering index avoids heap lookup.

questionText: Describe caching strategies: cache-aside, write-through, write-behind. When do you use each?
idealAnswer: Cache-aside (lazy loading): app checks cache, on miss loads from DB and populates. Resilient to cache failures. Write-through: write cache AND DB simultaneously. No stale reads but wasted entries. Write-behind: write cache only, async flush to DB. Lowest latency, data loss risk on crash. Redis TTL + cache-aside is most common. Cache stampede prevention: probabilistic early expiry or locks.

questionText: How would you implement rate limiting? Compare token bucket vs sliding window algorithms.
idealAnswer: Token bucket: N tokens added at rate R/sec. Allows bursting up to bucket size. Sliding window: track exact timestamps in last N seconds — more accurate, no boundary burst, expensive (O(r) memory). Sliding window counter: compromise using previous window count × overlap fraction. Redis implementation: sorted sets for sliding window. Return headers: X-RateLimit-Limit, X-RateLimit-Remaining, Retry-After.

questionText: When would you choose NoSQL over SQL? Explain the trade-offs.
idealAnswer: SQL: ACID, complex joins, structured schema, vertical scaling. NoSQL types: document (MongoDB), key-value (Redis), wide-column (Cassandra), graph (Neo4j). Choose NoSQL when: schema evolves rapidly, horizontal scaling needed, no complex joins, denormalization acceptable. CAP theorem: distributed SQL typically CP, Cassandra AP. NoSQL doesn't mean no schema — schema-on-read.

questionText: Explain ACID properties in databases with examples of each.
idealAnswer: Atomicity: all-or-nothing (half bank transfer never committed) — implemented via undo logs. Consistency: DB transitions between valid states, constraints always satisfied. Isolation: concurrent transactions don't interfere — levels: Read Committed, Repeatable Read, Serializable. Durability: committed data survives crashes via WAL (write-ahead log). Higher isolation = lower concurrency. MVCC enables non-blocking reads.

questionText: Why use a message queue? Compare Kafka vs RabbitMQ.
idealAnswer: Message queues decouple producers/consumers for async processing and load leveling. RabbitMQ: push-based, complex routing (exchanges), message deleted after consumption, good for task queues. Kafka: append-only log, pull-based, consumer groups, message retention + replay — best for event streaming, high throughput (millions/sec), data pipelines. At-least-once delivery common; exactly-once harder. Dead letter queues handle poison messages.

questionText: Compare WebSocket, Server-Sent Events, and HTTP long polling. Which for a chat app?
idealAnswer: Long Polling: client holds request open, high overhead. SSE: server→client one-way stream, auto-reconnect, text-based. WebSocket: full-duplex over single TCP connection, lowest latency, bidirectional. For chat: WebSocket best. Scaling: WebSocket needs sticky sessions or Redis pub/sub (Socket.io redis adapter) to work across multiple servers. SSE better for one-way notifications (activity feeds).

questionText: What are the trade-offs of microservices vs monolith? When is microservices the wrong choice?
idealAnswer: Monolith: simple deployment, local calls, shared memory, ACID across domains, easy debugging. Microservices: independent deployment, tech flexibility, fault isolation, independent scaling — but: network latency, distributed transactions (saga), service discovery, distributed tracing overhead. Wrong choice: small team, early product (domain not settled), no DevOps maturity. Strangler Fig pattern for incremental migration.

questionText: What is database connection pooling? How do you size a connection pool?
idealAnswer: Connection pooling reuses DB connections instead of creating new ones per request (expensive: TCP handshake + auth). Sizing formula (thread-based): num_cores × 2 + 1. For async Node.js: 10-20 connections — event loop isn't blocking. Too large: DB overloaded. Too small: queuing. Monitor pool wait time and active/idle connections. PgBouncer (PostgreSQL) acts as proxy pool.

questionText: What are the strategies for API versioning? What are the trade-offs?
idealAnswer: URL versioning (/v1/users): visible, easy to route but breaks RESTful resource identity. Header versioning (Accept: application/vnd.v2+json): cleaner URLs, harder to test. Query param (?version=2): simplest. Deprecation strategy: sunset headers, run old version 6-12 months. Breaking vs non-breaking changes. GraphQL alternative: additive schema evolution without versioning.

questionText: Best practices for error handling in a Node.js API. Distinguish operational vs programmer errors.
idealAnswer: Operational errors (expected): invalid input, network timeout — handle gracefully with proper HTTP status + structured error body. Programmer errors (bugs): null reference, logic errors — crash and restart. Error response: { error, message, requestId } — always include requestId for tracing. Never expose stack traces in production. Global: process.on('unhandledRejection'). Use try/catch on async routes.

questionText: Compare server-side sessions vs JWT. How would you implement sessions that survive server restarts?
idealAnswer: Server-side session: opaque session ID in cookie, session data in Redis. Can invalidate instantly. JWT: self-contained, stateless, scalable but can't revoke before expiry. Hybrid: opaque tokens with Redis lookup. Survive restarts: store sessions in Redis (not in-memory). Session fixation: regenerate ID after login. CSRF: SameSite=Strict + httpOnly + Secure cookie flags.

questionText: Explain the three pillars of observability: logs, metrics, traces. How do they work together?
idealAnswer: Logs: timestamped events (use structured JSON). Metrics: numerical measurements — use percentiles (p95, p99) NOT averages for latency. Prometheus + Grafana. Traces: track a request across services (spans with parent-child). Jaeger/Zipkin. Four Golden Signals: latency, traffic, errors, saturation. Correlation: alert on metric → find trace in logs via requestId. OpenTelemetry for vendor-neutral instrumentation.

questionText: Explain horizontal sharding. What are consistent hashing and resharding challenges?
idealAnswer: Sharding splits data across multiple DBs by shard key. Range-based: easy ranges but hot spots. Hash-based: even distribution, range queries expensive. Consistent hashing: nodes and keys on a ring, key routes to nearest clockwise node — adding/removing nodes only moves 1/n data. Resharding: expensive migration, use double-write + backfill. Cross-shard joins expensive. Avoid sharding: try read replicas and caching first.

questionText: Explain Docker. How does it differ from VMs? Best practices for production Dockerfiles.
idealAnswer: Docker containers share host kernel, use namespaces + cgroups for isolation. VMs: full OS per VM, GB size, slow startup. Containers: MB size, millisecond startup. Dockerfile best practices: multi-stage build (compile then copy artifact to minimal runtime), non-root user, minimal base image (alpine/distroless), .dockerignore, pin image versions, one process per container, COPY vs ADD.

questionText: When would you choose GraphQL over REST? What are GraphQL's main challenges?
idealAnswer: GraphQL advantages: client requests exactly what it needs (no over/under-fetching), single endpoint, self-documenting schema, multiple resources in one request. Challenges: N+1 query problem (solve with DataLoader batch loading), complex query cost analysis needed (DoS risk), no standard HTTP caching, file uploads awkward. Use GraphQL when: many clients with different data needs, mobile apps (bandwidth), rapid frontend iteration.

questionText: Explain load balancing algorithms and when to use sticky sessions.
idealAnswer: Round robin: even distribution, simple. Least connections: better for variable request duration. IP hash: same client → same server (sticky). Layer 4 (TCP-level) vs Layer 7 (HTTP-aware, inspect headers/path). Sticky sessions needed for in-memory sessions — but breaks horizontal scaling. Better: externalize sessions to Redis (no stickiness needed). Health checks: active (/health probe) vs passive (detect from traffic errors).

questionText: How would you implement an atomic bank transfer? What concurrency issues can occur?
idealAnswer: Use DB transaction: BEGIN; check balance; debit account A; credit account B; COMMIT. Add CHECK constraint (balance >= 0). Deadlock risk: two concurrent transfers A→B and B→A — prevent with consistent lock ordering or row-level locking (SELECT FOR UPDATE). With microservices: saga pattern with compensating transactions. Always validate: different accounts, positive amount, accounts exist.
